transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because… well, I’m embarrassed to even say it out loud, but what finally scared me enough to make the appointment is that after I eat too much, I’ve been going into the bathroom and making myself throw up. I tell myself it’s because I don’t want to gain weight, and at first I tried to convince myself it was just one bad choice, just something I did once and wouldn’t do again.

But it’s not feeling like that anymore. It’s gotten past being some one-time mistake, and that’s what really frightened me. I feel ashamed, and I don’t really know how to get a handle on it by myself.
How often have you been making yourself throw up after eating?

It’s… it’s most weeks now. I hate saying that, because part of me still wants to make it sound like it’s just every now and then, like I just slipped up once in a while. But if I’m being honest, for the past several months, there have been these times where I eat in secret and then afterward I feel panicked and ashamed, and I go and make myself sick.

So no, I don’t think I can honestly call it occasional anymore. It’s become enough of a pattern that I know it’s happening most weeks.
Do you often restrict the amount or types of food you eat between these episodes of bingeing and purging?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because I haven’t really kept track of it in an organized way or anything. I mean, I do think a lot about what I’m eating, probably more than I should, but I don’t know if I’d say I have a clear rule like, “I’m not allowed to eat this,” or “I can only eat that.” Some days I’ll tell myself I should be “good” or eat lighter, especially after I’ve had one of those episodes, but then other days it sort of falls apart.

So… yes, maybe in a loose way, but I’m not sure if it counts as restricting the way you mean. It’s more like I get anxious and try to compensate, and then I end up feeling pulled back and forth around food.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I know that probably sounds strange, because you’d think I’d know exactly, given how much I worry about it, but I don’t have a clear number to give you.

I don’t weigh myself in a very consistent way—sometimes I avoid the scale because I’m afraid of what it’ll say, and other times I check and then wish I hadn’t. So I can’t honestly say, “yes, I’ve lost this much” or “gained this much.” My clothes don’t feel dramatically different, at least not in a way I can trust, because some days I feel bigger no matter what I’m wearing.

So… I haven’t noticed a major, obvious change, but I’m also not sure I’m the best judge of it right now.
Do you have a persistent fear of gaining weight?

Yes… I do. I don’t like admitting that at my age, because it sounds vain or silly, but it’s there all the time in the back of my mind.

It can be something small, like if I’m getting dressed for church and my skirt feels tight at the waist or around my hips, I’ll just feel this awful sinking feeling. Then I start fussing with everything, trying on different things, looking in the mirror from the side, and suddenly I’m convinced I look bigger than I should. Or at work, if I catch my reflection in one of the store mirrors, especially from the side, it can just ruin my whole day. I’ll think, “Everyone can tell. Everyone can see I’ve let myself go.”

And I know people probably aren’t studying me like that, but in the moment it feels so real. I feel embarrassed, almost exposed. So yes, gaining weight scares me, but it’s not just the number. It’s how I think I look, and what I imagine other people are seeing.
Have you ever had episodes where you ate a large amount of food in a short time without later making yourself throw up?

Yes… there have been times like that. Not always followed by making myself throw up, if that’s what you mean.

It’s usually not like I sit down planning it. It’s more like if I’ve been out late, like after bridge night, or if I get home from a late shift and I’m tired and keyed up and the house is quiet, I’ll start with something that seems normal. Maybe I’ll warm up some leftover casserole, just a small dish, and then while it’s heating I’ll have a few crackers. Then I remember there are cookies I baked, and I’ll tell myself I’m just having one or two, and then suddenly I’ve eaten several. And then I might have ice cream too, standing there or sitting at the kitchen table, not even really enjoying it by the end.

And it’s definitely more than I would ever put on a plate in front of someone else. I’d be mortified if anyone saw the amount all together. It doesn’t feel like a regular meal or a snack. It feels like I’ve sort of crossed a line, but sometimes I don’t make myself throw up afterward. I just sit with that awful full feeling and regret it.
Do you think your weight or body shape is different from how others see you?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I know people probably don’t see me as harshly as I see myself, but it doesn’t feel that way when it’s happening.

Like before church, if I’m getting dressed and my skirt feels even a little tight, especially at the waist or hips, I can get completely stuck on it. I’ll keep pulling at it, turning sideways, trying to see if it shows, wondering if everyone will notice. And then I’m not just thinking, “This skirt is tight,” I’m thinking, “I look awful, I’ve let myself go, people can tell.”

The same thing happens at work sometimes. There are mirrors around the store, and if I catch myself from the side, it can ruin my whole day. I’ll see my shape and feel like it’s much bigger or worse than I expected, and then I assume other people are seeing that too. Even if nobody says anything, I feel exposed, like they must be noticing.

So yes, I suppose my mind makes it different. I don’t really trust what I see, but I still react to it like it’s the truth.
When you make yourself throw up, is it usually because you feel like you've eaten too much?

Yes… that’s usually the reason. It’s after I feel like I’ve eaten too much, like I’ve gone past what I meant to do, and then I panic about what it’s going to do to my weight.

That’s actually what scared me enough to come in. I’d eat too much, and then I’d go into the bathroom and make myself throw up so I wouldn’t gain weight. At first I tried to tell myself it was just a terrible mistake, something I wouldn’t do again, but it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time thing anymore. And I feel ashamed saying that out loud, but yes… it’s mostly because I feel too full and frightened that I’ll gain.
Do you think you would still make yourself throw up after eating if you didn't worry about your weight or body shape?

I don’t know… I suppose if I truly didn’t worry about gaining weight or how I looked, maybe I wouldn’t feel that same panic afterward. But honestly, that worry is so tied up in it that it’s hard for me to separate the two.

What happens is, after I eat too much, I start thinking right away, “I’ve ruined it, I’m going to gain, I can’t let this stay in me.” And then I end up going to the bathroom and making myself throw up. That’s the part that finally scared me into coming here, because it isn’t feeling like some one-time awful mistake anymore. It’s become something I do because I’m afraid of gaining weight, and I hate admitting that, but yes… that’s the reason.
Do you ever make yourself throw up for reasons other than trying to control your weight?

No… not really. At least, not that I can think of.

When it happens, it’s after I’ve eaten too much and I get scared about gaining weight. That’s the part that finally frightened me enough to come in here, because I’ll go into the bathroom and make myself throw up so it won’t stay in me, so it won’t turn into weight. I wish I could say it was because I felt sick or something like that, but it isn’t really that.

It’s more like I feel I’ve made a mistake by eating too much, and then I panic and think I have to undo it. And it’s gotten past where I can tell myself, “Oh, that was just one awful time.” It’s happened enough now that I know it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore. That’s what scares me.
Do you feel like you've lost control when you're eating during these episodes?

Yes… I do. That’s one of the parts that feels so upsetting, because it doesn’t feel like a normal decision anymore once it starts.

I’ll tell myself, “Just stop now, put it away, your husband might notice,” and I really do think that in the moment. It’s not like I’m completely unaware. But then it’s like I’m on automatic, and my hand is still going for one more thing, and then one more after that. I’ll be standing there thinking I should stop before it gets obvious, before he wonders what I’m doing, and at the same time I’m still eating.

It’s hard to explain without sounding foolish, because of course I know I’m the one doing it. But it feels like I’ve lost the brakes. Like the sensible part of me is there, saying, “Enough, stop,” and another part just keeps going anyway.
Do you think you would still eat large amounts of food in a short time if you didn't worry about gaining weight?

I’m not completely sure, because the fear of gaining weight is so mixed in with it for me. But if I’m being honest, the large amount part can start before I’m even thinking clearly about that.

Like after bridge night, or if I’ve worked a late shift and come home tired, I might start with just a little bit of leftover casserole, and then it turns into more casserole, and then I’ll see cookies I baked and have those, and then crackers, and then ice cream. All in one sitting. It’s not anything I would ever serve myself on a plate in front of someone else. I’d be mortified if anyone saw the actual amount all together.

So… I don’t know if I’d still do it without worrying about my weight. Maybe sometimes, yes, because it feels like once I start, I just keep going. But the worry afterward is a big part of what makes it feel so awful.
Do you feel like you're eating for pleasure or to satisfy hunger during these episodes, or is it more to cope with emotions?

I’m not completely sure how to separate those things, honestly. I don’t think it’s really pleasure in the way I’d normally mean pleasure, like sitting down and enjoying a nice meal. Sometimes the first few bites might feel comforting, or almost like a relief, but then it stops feeling like I’m enjoying it and starts feeling more frantic.

I don’t know that it’s hunger either, not most of the time. I might tell myself I’m hungry, or I might start because I haven’t eaten properly earlier, but once it gets going, it doesn’t feel like I’m calmly satisfying hunger. It’s more like I’m trying to quiet something down inside me, if that makes sense, though I couldn’t always tell you exactly what the feeling is. Sometimes I’m tired, or tense, or upset with myself, or just feeling sort of wound up, and food is there.

But I don’t always notice it in the moment. It’s usually afterward that I think, “What was that about?” During it, I’m not thinking very clearly. I’m just eating.
Do you always make yourself throw up after eating a large amount of food in a short time?

Not always, no… but more than I want to admit. That’s actually one of the things that finally scared me enough to come in here.

After I eat too much like that, I’ll start panicking about gaining weight, and then I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up. I hate even saying that out loud. At first I tried to tell myself it was just some awful one-time thing, like I’d lost my head and it wouldn’t happen again. But it hasn’t stayed that way. It’s happened enough now that I can’t pretend it was just a mistake or some strange accident.

I don’t do it after every single time, but when I’ve eaten a large amount, especially if I feel like I’ve really gone too far, the thought gets in my head that I have to undo it somehow. And then I’m in the bathroom, and afterward I feel ashamed and frightened by myself, because it feels like it’s becoming a pattern, not just a moment.
How often do you eat a large amount of food in a short time without making yourself throw up afterward?

I guess the times I don’t make myself throw up afterward are usually still the same kind of eating, if that makes sense. It’s not like it becomes a normal snack just because I don’t do that afterward.

Like I was saying, after a bridge night or if I’ve been on a late shift and I come home tired, I might start picking at leftover casserole, and then it isn’t just a little serving anymore. It turns into more casserole, then the cookies I baked, then crackers, then ice cream, all in one sitting. And when I think of it afterward, I feel sick with embarrassment because it’s much more than I would ever put on a plate if someone were sitting there with me.

As far as how often without making myself throw up… I’m not sure I can give you a neat number. It does happen, though. Sometimes I’m too worn out, or I sort of just go to bed feeling awful, or I sit there telling myself I won’t do anything else and try to pretend it didn’t happen. But the large amount of food part is still there. It’s still that same out-of-control feeling, even if I don’t end up in the bathroom afterward.
Do you think your desire to make yourself throw up after eating is more about undoing the calories or about relieving the feeling of being out of control?

I think… if I’m being really honest, it’s mostly about the calories and gaining weight. That’s the thought that gets loud in my head after I’ve eaten too much — that I’ve done something terrible and now I have to undo it somehow. I start thinking, “If I don’t get rid of it, it’s going to stay in me, and I’m going to gain weight,” and then I end up in the bathroom.

But it’s not completely separate from the out-of-control feeling either. Because feeling out of control is what makes me panic, and then throwing up feels like this awful way of trying to take control back. Not in a calm or sensible way, obviously. It doesn’t feel sensible at all. It feels desperate.

What finally scared me into coming in is that it’s not just some one-time mistake anymore. I kept telling myself, “That was the last time,” or “That only happened because I ate too much and got frightened,” but then after another time of eating too much, I’d be back in the bathroom making myself throw up so I wouldn’t gain weight. And afterward I feel ashamed, but in the moment it’s like that fear takes over.
Do you currently use any other methods to compensate for the calories you consume, such as excessive exercise or fasting?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I don’t think I have some whole list of things I do on purpose the way I’ve described the throwing up. That’s the main thing I’ve been frightened about.

With exercise, I wouldn’t say I’m doing some extreme routine or anything like that. I’m on my feet a fair amount with work, but that’s not the same as me deliberately going out and exercising for hours to make up for food. And fasting… I don’t know. I might tell myself I should “be good” the next day or eat less because I feel guilty, but I’m not sure if that counts as fasting the way you mean it.

So I guess the honest answer is, I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself using other specific methods in the same clear way. The one I know I’m doing, and the one that scares me, is making myself throw up.
Is your desire to make yourself throw up after eating mainly to prevent weight gain or to make up for the calories you've consumed?

Yes… mainly to prevent weight gain. That’s the part that scares me because after I eat too much, it’s like my mind goes straight to, “I can’t let this stay in me.” I’m not really thinking about it in some organized, logical way, like counting every calorie right then, but it is about making up for what I ate and being afraid it will turn into weight.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve been going into the bathroom afterward and making myself throw up so I won’t gain weight. And I kept trying to tell myself it was just a one-time mistake, or that I wouldn’t do it again, but it’s not feeling like that anymore. It’s gotten to where after I eat too much, that urge to undo it is there, and I feel ashamed saying that out loud.
Do you think your eating habits and purging behavior are significantly interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Yes… I think it is, though I hate admitting that because from the outside I’m still doing the things I’m supposed to do. I still go to work, I still go to church, I still play bridge, so part of me wants to say, “Well, I’m functioning, so maybe it’s not that bad.”

But it’s affecting how I go through the day. I catch myself planning around food in a way I didn’t used to. Like thinking ahead about what might be served, or whether I can avoid certain foods, or whether I’ll be able to get home and be alone afterward if I feel panicky. And that makes social things feel… tense. They’re not just enjoyable anymore.

Even with people I care about, I’m sort of half-present sometimes, because I’m thinking about what I ate or what I might eat or how I’m going to handle it later. So yes, I’m still showing up, but it’s taking up too much room in my head, and it’s starting to shape my life more than I want it to.

Yes… I do. That’s one of the parts that feels so upsetting, because it doesn’t feel like a normal decision anymore once it starts.

I’ll tell myself, “Just stop now, put it away, your husband might notice,” and I really do think that in the moment. It’s not like I’m completely unaware. But then it’s like I’m on automatic, and my hand is still going for one more thing, and then one more after that. I’ll be standing there thinking I should stop before it gets obvious, before he wonders what I’m doing, and at the same time I’m still eating.

It’s hard to explain without sounding foolish, because of course I know I’m the one doing it. But it feels like I’ve lost the brakes. Like the sensible part of me is there, saying, “Enough, stop,” and another part just keeps going anyway.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a fear of gaining weight or a lack of control while eating
doctor.question: Do you think you would still eat large amounts of food in a short time if you didn't worry about gaining weight?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: After a bridge night or a late shift, I might come home and eat leftover casserole, cookies I baked, crackers, and ice cream all in one sitting, much more than I’d ever put on a plate in front of anyone.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly asking about whether episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short time would still occur, which matches the large-amount binge eating symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure, because the fear of gaining weight is so mixed in with it for me. But if I’m being honest, the large amount part can start before I’m even thinking clearly about that.

Like after bridge night, or if I’ve worked a late shift and come home tired, I might start with just a little bit of leftover casserole, and then it turns into more casserole, and then I’ll see cookies I baked and have those, and then crackers, and then ice cream. All in one sitting. It’s not anything I would ever serve myself on a plate in front of someone else. I’d be mortified if anyone saw the actual amount all together.

So… I don’t know if I’d still do it without worrying about my weight. Maybe sometimes, yes, because it feels like once I start, I just keep going. But the worry afterward is a big part of what makes it feel so awful.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is driven by a desire to eat or by emotional factors
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're eating for pleasure or to satisfy hunger during these episodes, or is it more to cope with emotions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation or emotional trigger for eating episodes, which is not directly covered by the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to separate those things, honestly. I don’t think it’s really pleasure in the way I’d normally mean pleasure, like sitting down and enjoying a nice meal. Sometimes the first few bites might feel comforting, or almost like a relief, but then it stops feeling like I’m enjoying it and starts feeling more frantic.

I don’t know that it’s hunger either, not most of the time. I might tell myself I’m hungry, or I might start because I haven’t eaten properly earlier, but once it gets going, it doesn’t feel like I’m calmly satisfying hunger. It’s more like I’m trying to quiet something down inside me, if that makes sense, though I couldn’t always tell you exactly what the feeling is. Sometimes I’m tired, or tense, or upset with myself, or just feeling sort of wound up, and food is there.

But I don’t always notice it in the moment. It’s usually afterward that I think, “What was that about?” During it, I’m not thinking very clearly. I’m just eating.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's binge eating is always followed by purging
doctor.question: Do you always make yourself throw up after eating a large amount of food in a short time?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: What finally scared me into coming in is that after I eat too much, I’ve been making myself throw up in the bathroom so I won’t gain weight, and it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether large eating episodes are followed by self-induced vomiting, which directly concerns purging as a compensatory behavior.

patient.answer:
Not always, no… but more than I want to admit. That’s actually one of the things that finally scared me enough to come in here.

After I eat too much like that, I’ll start panicking about gaining weight, and then I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up. I hate even saying that out loud. At first I tried to tell myself it was just some awful one-time thing, like I’d lost my head and it wouldn’t happen again. But it hasn’t stayed that way. It’s happened enough now that I can’t pretend it was just a mistake or some strange accident.

I don’t do it after every single time, but when I’ve eaten a large amount, especially if I feel like I’ve really gone too far, the thought gets in my head that I have to undo it somehow. And then I’m in the bathroom, and afterward I feel ashamed and frightened by myself, because it feels like it’s becoming a pattern, not just a moment.

doctor.intent: determine frequency of binge eating without subsequent purging
doctor.question: How often do you eat a large amount of food in a short time without making yourself throw up afterward?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: After a bridge night or a late shift, I might come home and eat leftover casserole, cookies I baked, crackers, and ice cream all in one sitting, much more than I’d ever put on a plate in front of anyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about episodes of eating a large amount of food in a short time, with a specific clarification about whether they occur without vomiting afterward.

patient.answer:
I guess the times I don’t make myself throw up afterward are usually still the same kind of eating, if that makes sense. It’s not like it becomes a normal snack just because I don’t do that afterward.

Like I was saying, after a bridge night or if I’ve been on a late shift and I come home tired, I might start picking at leftover casserole, and then it isn’t just a little serving anymore. It turns into more casserole, then the cookies I baked, then crackers, then ice cream, all in one sitting. And when I think of it afterward, I feel sick with embarrassment because it’s much more than I would ever put on a plate if someone were sitting there with me.

As far as how often without making myself throw up… I’m not sure I can give you a neat number. It does happen, though. Sometimes I’m too worn out, or I sort of just go to bed feeling awful, or I sit there telling myself I won’t do anything else and try to pretend it didn’t happen. But the large amount of food part is still there. It’s still that same out-of-control feeling, even if I don’t end up in the bathroom afterward.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a fear of gaining weight or by a lack of control over eating
doctor.question: Do you think your desire to make yourself throw up after eating is more about undoing the calories or about relieving the feeling of being out of control?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: What finally scared me into coming in is that after I eat too much, I’ve been making myself throw up in the bathroom so I won’t gain weight, and it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind making herself throw up after eating, which directly concerns purging as a compensatory behavior to prevent weight gain.

patient.answer:
I think… if I’m being really honest, it’s mostly about the calories and gaining weight. That’s the thought that gets loud in my head after I’ve eaten too much — that I’ve done something terrible and now I have to undo it somehow. I start thinking, “If I don’t get rid of it, it’s going to stay in me, and I’m going to gain weight,” and then I end up in the bathroom.

But it’s not completely separate from the out-of-control feeling either. Because feeling out of control is what makes me panic, and then throwing up feels like this awful way of trying to take control back. Not in a calm or sensible way, obviously. It doesn’t feel sensible at all. It feels desperate.

What finally scared me into coming in is that it’s not just some one-time mistake anymore. I kept telling myself, “That was the last time,” or “That only happened because I ate too much and got frightened,” but then after another time of eating too much, I’d be back in the bathroom making myself throw up so I wouldn’t gain weight. And afterward I feel ashamed, but in the moment it’s like that fear takes over.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with bulimia nervosa or another eating disorder
doctor.question: Do you currently use any other methods to compensate for the calories you consume, such as excessive exercise or fasting?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about other compensatory methods like excessive exercise or fasting, but the symptom profile only covers purging by vomiting and does not include exercise or fasting.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I don’t think I have some whole list of things I do on purpose the way I’ve described the throwing up. That’s the main thing I’ve been frightened about.

With exercise, I wouldn’t say I’m doing some extreme routine or anything like that. I’m on my feet a fair amount with work, but that’s not the same as me deliberately going out and exercising for hours to make up for food. And fasting… I don’t know. I might tell myself I should “be good” the next day or eat less because I feel guilty, but I’m not sure if that counts as fasting the way you mean it.

So I guess the honest answer is, I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself using other specific methods in the same clear way. The one I know I’m doing, and the one that scares me, is making myself throw up.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is primarily driven by a fear of gaining weight or a desire to compensate for calories consumed
doctor.question: Is your desire to make yourself throw up after eating mainly to prevent weight gain or to make up for the calories you've consumed?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: What finally scared me into coming in is that after I eat too much, I’ve been making myself throw up in the bathroom so I won’t gain weight, and it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about the motivation for making herself throw up after eating, which is purging to prevent weight gain or compensate for calories.

patient.answer:
Yes… mainly to prevent weight gain. That’s the part that scares me because after I eat too much, it’s like my mind goes straight to, “I can’t let this stay in me.” I’m not really thinking about it in some organized, logical way, like counting every calorie right then, but it is about making up for what I ate and being afraid it will turn into weight.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve been going into the bathroom afterward and making myself throw up so I won’t gain weight. And I kept trying to tell myself it was just a one-time mistake, or that I wouldn’t do it again, but it’s not feeling like that anymore. It’s gotten to where after I eat too much, that urge to undo it is there, and I feel ashamed saying that out loud.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with purging disorder or other specified feeding or eating disorder
doctor.question: Do you think your eating habits and purging behavior are significantly interfering with your daily life or relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for work, church, and bridge, but I’ve started planning my day around avoiding certain foods or getting home alone afterward. It makes social things feel tense instead of enjoyable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the eating and purging are significantly interfering with daily life or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it is, though I hate admitting that because from the outside I’m still doing the things I’m supposed to do. I still go to work, I still go to church, I still play bridge, so part of me wants to say, “Well, I’m functioning, so maybe it’s not that bad.”

But it’s affecting how I go through the day. I catch myself planning around food in a way I didn’t used to. Like thinking ahead about what might be served, or whether I can avoid certain foods, or whether I’ll be able to get home and be alone afterward if I feel panicky. And that makes social things feel… tense. They’re not just enjoyable anymore.

Even with people I care about, I’m sort of half-present sometimes, because I’m thinking about what I ate or what I might eat or how I’m going to handle it later. So yes, I’m still showing up, but it’s taking up too much room in my head, and it’s starting to shape my life more than I want it to.
